newsitem.title: USA: Tour sees better yields, quality in U.S. SRW wheat.
newsitem.headline: Tour sees better yields, quality in U.S. SRW wheat.

text.p: Better yields and quality were expected from this year's U.S. soft red winter wheat crop than the 1996 supply after crop scouts this week inspected wheat fields from Ohio to Arkansas.
"I was relieved because this crop on the whole will be better than last year," said Rick Waite, Chattanooga, Tenn-based flour milling quality assurance manager for Cargill Inc.
The three-day annual Wheat Quality Council-sponsored soft red winter wheat tour ended Wednesday with participants finding healthy wheat in Arkansas and Ohio, but some disease in Illinois fields.

The tour traveled through southeast Missouri and northern Arkansas Wednesday and participants estimated potential yields there at 60 bushels per acre. That compared with the 1996 average yield of about 48 bushels for southeast Missouri and nearly 54 bushels for portions of northern Arkansas.
Tillers were estimated at 60 per square foot this year, which was near the 61 count last year. Last year was the first year the tour ventured into that area.
"The soft wheat quality this year will be better than last year," said Cargill's Waite. He noted that SRW wheat in northwestern Ohio and Arkansas was very good.
"In Arkansas not much can happen. There was very little damage. Wheat berries were full and mature and were ready to be cut," he said.
In northwest Ohio, which the tour covered Monday, the wheat was not as mature.
"Thus things can happen before the mid-July harvest," Waite said. "But if the weather holds and is warm, sunny and breezy, than it will be a beautiful crop."
Waite said he saw the worst damage in central Illinois where light to moderate disease pressure was evident from fusiarium head scab and glume blotch rust.
"It would be difficult (to assess) how significant the damage is. But that crop is expected to be better than last year," he said.

The tour began Monday and went through northwest Ohio, southern Michigan, northeast Indiana, central and southern Illinois, Missouri and Arkansas. Participants included grain merchandisers, flour millers, USDA officials, agronomists, and agriculture reporters.
Tour leader Jim Quinton said he did not see scab in Arkansas or Missouri wheat.
"Scab was a non-issue in the bootheel of Missouri and in Arkansas," Quinton said.
But, like Waite, Quinton did report scab in some Illinois wheat fields.
Scab is a fungal disease that attacks the wheat kernel. Glume blotch also a fungal disease.
